item.title: I stopped using my TV's USB port as a power supply for streaming devices
item.itunes:title: I stopped using my TV's USB port as a power supply for streaming devices
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I'm fed up with streaming sticks that draw power from my TV's USB port. You can do a lot with a TV's USB port, but it's often underpowered for streaming devices with demanding power needs. This is especially true with older sets. It's convenient if it works since I don't have to plug it into the wall or power strip. But a TV's port isn't always a reliable power source.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

New devices with direct-power connectivity (a cable that plugs into the USB port to power the stick) require more power than the port can provide. Depending on the TV, I get low-power errors, random crashes, or the stick won't turn on. It's not a universal problem, but it's broad enough to be concerning.

TV sets aren't meant to run streaming computer devices

Most USB ports are underpowered

Your TV's USB port is meant for low-power actions like inserting a flash drive to view photos or other local media. I have last year's Roku HD streaming stick and the Fire TV 4K (3rd-generation), and both have direct-power cables that draw power from the TV's USB port. Sure, it is convenient; it eliminates a wall wart mess (plugging device chargers into wall outlets), hanging cords, tangled cords, and keeps things clean for wall-mounted sets. But you might plug it in, and nothing will happen.

Many TV sets' USB ports are underpowered and offer a trickle of energy — usually around 0.5A. But the new Fire TV Stick and Roku HD Stick need 5V/1A to run, and if they don't work, the companies recommend plugging them into the included wall adapter anyway. That happened to me when I plugged in my Roku HD Stick into an older 4K TV earlier this year. I was instantly irked because I had to pull out the wall adapter and plug it into the power strip surge protector.

Another problem with using the set's USB port is that the device may not stay charged when the TV is powered off, and will cold-boot every session. That can cause long delays that are simply unacceptable. Low-power messages, random reboots, and crashes in the middle of streaming can occur. USB port power output varies wildly between models. Check your set's USB rating before buying a device if you plan to use direct USB power to make sure it will work.

I replaced my Fire TV Stick with a mini PC, and now my TV does things Amazon never intended

Upgrading to a high-quality streaming experience.

9
By  Samir Makwana

Cold boots and random crash interruptions

Turning off the TV powers off the USB port, and inconsistent power causes crashes

If your TV's USB port does power your stick, that's great. However, you might have to deal with cold boots. That's when you turn off your TV; it also powers off the stick. So, each time you fire it up, it takes longer to complete its boot cycle. That creates an unnecessary delay that can get really annoying when you're done for the day and just want to stream Netflix. If you only run one streaming stick, some sets let you keep the port powered even when the TV is off. Check your TV's power or system settings to find it and set it to "Always on."

However, the stick can power on and seem to work. But a TV's USB port may supply too little or inconsistent power to the streaming device. That can cause all sorts of issues, like buffering, random crashes and reboots, menu freeze-ups, and more. When that happens, Roku and Amazon recommend plugging their sticks into their included power adapters anyway.

Only one port for multiple streaming devices

A solution to problematic math

Another issue is that I have multiple streaming sticks and only one power USB port on my set. Also, with the number of streaming devices I have, my surge protector gets clogged up fast. So I have to plug them in directly or get creative. My mind immediately went to using one of my powered USB hubs. This is cool for a geek, but it shouldn't have to be the solution for an average consumer. A similar situation happened to my aunt and uncle, and they had to call me for help.

With a powered USB-A hub, I plug the hub's power adapter into my power strip, connect the device's power cords, and plug the sticks into the HDMI ports I want to use. When looking for a powered hub, consider how many devices you have and what they need. I used a cheap Sarbrent 4-port hub with a 5V, 2.5A power adapter, and plugged the USB Type-A port into the hub instead of the TV's port. But the power capacity is shared across all ports. It doesn't mean each port has adequate power for all connected devices.

Still, I can successfully power my Amazon Fire TV Stick and Roku HD device without a problem. I even connected an Onn 4K Google TV streamer and multiple external drives to create a locally hosted network server with the budget box. The Onn streamer and drives worked well, with no device interruptions. A hub offers more ports for devices and can solve issues with underpowered USB ports on TVs in general. So, even if you have one stick and an underpowered USB port on your TV, a hub works and provides headroom for expansion.

Don't plug the hub into the set's USB port. That can send power back into the port and damage it and the TV. Leave your set's USB port out of the chain for this configuration.

Direct power for streaming sticks is a convenient problem

My new TV can power a new direct-power streaming stick with no hiccups. However, on older sets, the sticks introduce problems or don't turn on at all. However, since I have multiple streaming devices and don't want tons of chargers in my power strip, I use a powered hub to get the job done. It only requires plugging in one device instead of four or more. Plus, the USB port on my set stays open if I need it.

Sabrent 4-port USB Hub (HB-UM43)
$15 at Amazon
ii

item.title: The cheapest upgrade for an old Raspberry Pi isn't a new and more expensive Raspberry Pi
item.itunes:title: The cheapest upgrade for an old Raspberry Pi isn't a new and more expensive Raspberry Pi
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Raspberry Pi you bought to try out might start to feel slow and limiting over time. You might not feel the same excitement you did at first. You might also hit visible roadblocks that push you to upgrade to a better board with higher specs. However, in most cases, you can actually do a little overhaul yourself and try to fix things.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Rather than impulsively buying a new board, inspect the problems and make small tweaks that can make a big difference. I highly suggest doing and testing the impact of minor upgrades like cooling, storage, and power before buying the newest Raspberry Pi. SBC prices aren't as low as they used to be, which is another reason to make do with what you have.

A new SBC won't magically make your projects better

Hardware limitations still apply

Before suggesting anything, I want to make one thing very clear. If your projects are suffering from severely low performance or memory capacity, minor upgrades won't help. You cannot get the same experience of running a tool like Nextcloud or Home Assistant on two very different Raspberry Pis. Adding an SSD or cooling hardware won't make a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W match the performance of a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B or Raspberry Pi 5.

5 reasons your Raspberry Pi isn’t as fast as it should be (and how to fix it)

Even a Raspberry Pi needs some fine-tuning to stay in tip-top form

By  Ayush Pande

For example, if you are using an SD card on a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B for a project that requires extensive I/O operations. A tool like Nextcloud, a Frigate server, or a Kopia setup needs to manage a database and logs, and it can struggle on an SD card. Running multiple demanding Docker containers can also work painfully slowly if you base everything on the SD card. Overheating can also degrade performance, and an inadequate power supply can cause disconnections, undervoltage errors, and unexplained reboots.

Fix storage first

SD cards aren’t the optimal solution

The solution is to upgrade the storage setup with a USB SSD. Shifting everything from the SD card to the USB is a much wiser approach. Each Raspberry Pi model has a different SD card and USB port, so performance will vary. The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W uses the SD High Speed (SD 2.0) interface with write speeds of about 20MB/s. Using a USB SSD with it bumps up the write speeds to 35MB/s. Of course, the tier of an SD card and SSD also matters, but there’s a stark difference between the two.

The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B has a much faster SDR50 interface, and a good SD card can give you about 40MB/s write performance. But ditching the SDR50 interface for an SSD is a major win because the board comes with a couple of USB 3.0 ports. So, you can connect an internal SSD with a SATA-to-USB enclosure and enjoy upwards of 250MB/s write speeds. For a camera monitoring setup or a media server with extensive metadata management, this kind of faster storage is a boon.

PCIe 5.0 SSDs are the fastest drives I've ever used, yet nothing I do actually got faster

I didn't expect everything to get twice as fast, but I also didn't expect what I got

3
By  Tanveer Singh

Lastly, the Raspberry Pi 5 board doubles the SD card interface speeds with a 104 MB/s bus rate, but the real power is the PCIe NVMe SSD support. It also supports AI HAT modules, and pairing it with a low-memory version can actually help you run LLM projects and anything else AI-related. Some HAT modules have onboard memory, and you can even get by with a 4GB board for specific AI projects.

This is exclusive to the Raspberry Pi 5 series, which is why it's the most expensive board on the roster. It’s even possible to unlock Gen 3 data transfer speeds, which can push your read/write performance closer to 1GB/s. Even if you stick to the default PCIe Gen 2 interface, the 350–400 MB/s (or even more) write speeds are still way beyond the USB 3.0 SSD performance.

Read/write speeds aren't the only benefit of switching to an external storage device. SD cards are prone to corruption, and it's disheartening to see them fail. I've witnessed it twice and don't suggest using an SD card for storing anything important. It's wise to leverage the available USB ports or the dedicated PCIe slot if you have a Raspberry Pi 5. SSDs are much more reliable and actually built to handle continuous I/O operations.

Power and cooling also matter

A scorching, underpowered SBC is no good

The tiny credit-card computer might look like it would run off a 10W USB phone charger, but that doesn’t apply to all the models. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W can work with 10W, but a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B will fall short of power in some situations. If you connect multiple USB drives to it, the 10W power supply will result in abrupt disconnections and reboots. Similarly, a Raspberry Pi 5 needs a 25W power supply, so your 15–20W phone chargers limit the maximum USB power available to other devices.

Some Raspberry Pi cases, like the aluminum ones, are expensive. But an acrylic case with fans and proper heat sinks can remove a lot of heat from the board. So, you can extend the board's lifespan while running it 24/7. I use inexpensive cases, and they help keep the SBCs cool. You can find acrylic cases with a fan and heat sink combo for $5-10.

11 ways to maximize your Raspberry Pi’s performance

If you want to really get the most out of your Raspberry Pi, these tips will help maximize its performance.

By  Jeff Butts

This is a standard protection measure, and you can even check the current temps with CLI tools. DietPi displays the current temperature on the dashboard, but you can use the temperature monitoring tool included in the official Raspberry Pi OS as well.

Evaluate SBC purchases

Don't rush to buy a new SBC because your current one doesn't work. Most projects benefit the most from a storage, cooling, or power upgrade. I would suggest buying a new SBC only if the current one has hardware constraints like low memory or processor performance. Even then, I would strongly suggest an old thin client over something like a $45 Raspberry Pi 5 (excluding $40 accessories). But a new Raspberry Pi only if you need the GPIO connectivity along with the faster SoC.

Raspberry Pi 5
CPU
Arm Cortex-A76 (quad-core, 2.4GHz)
Memory
Up to 8GB LPDDR4X SDRAM

The Raspberry Pi is back, and the fifth iteration of the SBC is a lot more capable than the older models. From a new quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 CPU, support for dual monitor setups at 4K 60Hz, and a dedicated power button, there's a lot to love about this palm-sized computer.

item.title: My local LLM turns my voice notes into to-do items automatically, and nothing falls through the cracks
item.itunes:title: My local LLM turns my voice notes into to-do items automatically, and nothing falls through the cracks
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My PC is usually a mess of windows, apps, browser tabs, and half-finished things I'm supposed to remember. In fact, if I had a dollar for every time a thought appeared while I was working only to disappear the next minute, I could probably hire an assistant to stay on top of every task for me. I'll think of something I need to do, tell myself I’ll get to it in a minute, and then spend the next hour wondering what it was.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've tried dictation tools, but they solve a problem I don't really have. I don't need my computer to type faster, after all. I need it to understand what I'm saying when I'm thinking out loud and turn that rambling mess into something useful. So I ended up building exactly that — a completely local voice-to-task system that listens, understands, and pulls the things I actually need to remember out of the noise.

After a year of self-hosting LLMs, I realized the real bottleneck isn’t the GPU

Hardware is just the entry fee for local intelligence.

20
By  Yash Patel

The one thing I didn't need was better dictation

Two models do the job better than just one

When I'm working, I have a browser window, Slack, Discord, an editor, file explorer, and whatever game or benchmark I'm testing scattered across two displays. A thought will inevitably appear somewhere in that chaos, I'll remember that I have to email someone, or test a setting later, or download something that I'll need the next day or a few hours later. I promise myself I'll remember it, of course, but that's pretty much a legally binding guarantee that I won't.

The setup is surprisingly simple once I stopped trying to make one model do everything. When I record a voice note, Whisper transcribes it locally, and that transcript gets passed to Qwen running through llama.cpp. Whisper's job is strictly to hear me, while it's Qwen's job to figure out what I actually meant and turn it into proper structured tasks for me to be able to refer to.

I use Qwen 3.5-9B with the Q4_K_M quantization, simply because it runs perfectly on my 12GB GPU without taking up too much space. Paired with Whisper, my to-do tasks are created, from start to finish, while using just 7GB of VRAM on my RTX 4070 Ti.

One important part in the pipeline I ensured was that my LLM wasn't going to also play calendar administrator. As such, it just extracts the task, works out the intended timing, and then returns the structured data, while the actual date calculation happens all in code. This matters because I'd rather trust a few lines of deterministic code with "tomorrow" stamped next to it instead of an LLM that occasionally decides that tomorrow is a philosophical concept.

The result is much closer to what I originally wanted. A voice note saying "I need to order snacks for the weekend party, thoroughly clean the house, and clean the air fryer" comes back as three separate items, with their times attached, and the list automatically sorted chronologically. I don't have to reinterpret my own voice note later.

Trying to self-host LLMs made me realize local AI has a friction problem, not a quality problem

Think of it as the Linux desktop problem, all over again

30
By  Samarveer Singh

Cleanliness is the most important part of the process

Too many moving parts would've made this entire thing useless

Now, when I first drew a rough outline of this entire pipeline in my head, it had too many moving parts. I'd have to open the sound recorder app on Windows, talk into the mic about all my pending tasks and their deadlines, and then save the recording. I'd then have to prepare Qwen 3.5-9B on a llama server locally, before ensuring that I point the Whisper engine in the right direction to pick up the clip I'd just saved.

That was three separate windows (recorder, terminal watching the model server, and the script itself), none of which talk to each other unless I personally walked the file from one to the next. Technically speaking, it worked, but in the way that a car with no seats "technically" drives. In practice, transcribing my voice notes became too much of a chore, which was ironic, since my original intent was to solve a chore. I had to make it all neater and condense it into one single package if possible so I'd actually use it past the novelty of the first day.

As such, I wrapped it all up into one single Python file that started my server, connected the Whisper engine, enabled sound-recording, and transcribed everything while converting it into actionable items, all neatly packed into a GUI on my desktop. This was how I finally made the entire process usable, since I never had to juggle three separate PowerShell windows while keeping track of what prerequisites each function in the pipeline needed. The to-do items simply display in batches of six right on my desktop, like a sticky note I can drag and drop wherever I need.

I stopped typing to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for a week, and discovered a better way to use AI

I gave my fingers a break and my AI chats got better

4
By  Mahnoor Faisal

My GPU does the heavy lifting but the transcribing happens on the CPU

It's much simpler this way

I'd be lying if I said that it all worked in the very first try, because it did not. My audio libraries were impossible to find for faster-whisper, and the Whisper engine was unable to find my Nvidia math libraries, no matter how many times I downloaded them. Ultimately, I offloaded the entire process to my CPU, which only made practical sense in this case — while dealing with 20-30-second voice notes, the CPU itself finished in seconds, so I never felt the need to force my GPU to take over. It was pretty content serving up the models and holding them in its VRAM.

Claude Code helped immensely here, helping me code iteration after iteration that eventually let me select the voice input method right in the GUI. It even gave me a toggle for off-loading both Whisper and Qwen models to completely free up my GPU without closing my voice-note-taking app, and just pressing the record button the next time would start up the server and the models again if I remembered something worth adding to my to-do list.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

Automation was never the point — I just want my thoughts to stay on my PC

The biggest reason I kept this local is also the simplest — these are my thoughts, and there's no reason they need to leave my machine just to become a to-do list. I spend 14 hours on my PC, and my microphone is always right beside my desk. There’s no cloud API sitting in the middle and no subscription waiting to turn a tiny productivity problem into another monthly bill.

The system isn't perfect, though. There's the occasional name that's misheard or mangled, and there's also a small warm-up pause when I bring the GPU back online. However, these are acceptable trade-offs for something that works. Single-model audio systems will eventually make this even cleaner, but for now, two specialised models are more than enough.

llama.cpp

Llama.cpp is an open-source framework that runs large language models locally on your computer.

item.itunes:title: 4 things One UI 9 turned on behind my back, and I switched off every one
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have been a long-term iPhone user, and I have kept a secondary Android phone with me. I always loved stock Android experiences, and one of the reasons for loving it was how bloated UIs like Samsung’s old TouchWiz and Xiaomi’s MIUI were. But when Samsung announced One UI in 2018, things started changing for me.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The first time I personally used One UI was on my Galaxy A8, my sister’s hand-me-down phone. Since then, I have upgraded to many Galaxy phones, and today, I am using the Galaxy S25. In the last seven years, I have customized One UI to my liking, but when I updated from One UI 8.5 to 9.0 last month, it changed a few settings I deliberately set on my Galaxy.

My phone forgot which keyboard I actually use

Samsung replaced my preferred keyboard

There are a few things on a smartphone that you keep for years only because of habit. For me, that thing is Gboard. I have been using it for, I don't even know, how many years. As far as I remember, I never used any other keyboard on my Android phones. It has always been on my Android devices, not only Samsung but others too.

After the new 9.0 update, everything was smooth, and the new features were alright, but when I opened the keyboard to search for something, I noticed that it wasn’t the same keyboard anymore. My first thought was maybe it was a new Gboard update. But almost everything was different, so I checked and found out that after the update, it was reset to the Samsung keyboard.

I changed it back to Gboard and decided to scout through the settings to see what else was changed after the update.

I almost wrote off these Galaxy One UI 9 features as gimmicks, but they genuinely made my life better

They almost run my daily routine now

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Maximum protection became the bare minimum

One UI 9 lowered my battery protection

In my line of work, I'm at my desk almost 90% of the time, so my phones and laptops are always plugged in. Even though most phones and laptops are quite intelligent when it comes to smart charging, I am the kind of person who always takes one extra step to be more cautious.

Both my primary iPhone 16 and secondary Galaxy S25 have adaptive charging capabilities, but I still limit the charging to a certain level. In One UI, the setting is known as Maximum Battery Protection, and it lets me limit the charging percentage between 80 and 95. So, I always keep the setting at 90%.

While scouting for the settings One UI 9.0 changed, it was the first setting I noticed. The update turned on Basic Battery Protection. I switched from basic protection back to maximum with a 90% limit. Basic protection means the system lets the charger charge to 100% and then stops charging; once the battery percentage drops to 95%, it starts charging again.

A security feature that would block my own apps

My debugging workflow hit a security roadblock

On weekdays, I am a full-time technical writer and editor, and on weekends, I am a software developer. I started with web apps, and these days, I am taking a keen interest in mobile application development, mostly Android apps. Android Studio does offer Android phone emulators, but I always try to test my apps on a real phone, and that is usually my Galaxy S25.

A normal Android device has a protection where it doesn't allow APK files from unknown sources. We all know that and keep that permission off, but Samsung adds an extra layer to that setting. One UI has an Auto Blocker feature, and when it is turned on, it not only blocks apps from untrusted sources but also blocks USB cable commands, non-official software updates, and more.

For a developer like me, this means I can’t install my debug APKs and test. So, I usually keep the setting off, and it was off in One UI 8.5. But when I checked after the update, I found it on. I switched it off and moved on. Still, for a normal user, it is one of the features to keep always on.

Samsung DeX finally clicked for me when I stopped treating it like a phone

DeX won't replace your laptop — but it doesn't need to.

By  Shekhar Vaidya

Technically impressive doesn't always mean visually better

I still don't want Super HDR

Super HDR is Samsung’s version of Google’s Ultra HDR. Samsung implemented it in all Galaxy flagships starting with the S24 series. On paper, it has really impressive features like detailed highlights and shadows, a vivid display boost, and more, but honestly, I don’t like it.

Before you jump to conclusions and criticize me in the comments, let me be very clear: this is my personal choice, and I don’t like it because of a few events that happened to me in the past. I was using the S23 FE before getting the S25, and it didn’t have Super HDR.

After I got the new S25, I was scrolling through Instagram Reels one night when one reel’s brightness suddenly spiked. I thought maybe adaptive brightness was acting up, so I ignored it and kept scrolling. After a few reels, it happened again. Surprisingly, it was only the video area, not the app UI or phone UI.

So, I Googled it and found that the "flashbang" happened because the creator uploaded the reel in Ultra HDR/HDR format, and since Super HDR was supported in my S25, I got the flashbang. That was when, despite the impressive features, I turned it off. But the One UI 9.0 update somehow reset that setting and turned Super HDR back on.

I disabled it again, so I won’t get another flashbang while scrolling reels at night.

This old Galaxy phone became my third WAN port, and it actually works

The cheapest backup line I never planned for.

4
By  Shekhar Vaidya

Trust the update, check the settings

Over the years, Samsung has really improved One UI, and it's no doubt one of the best Android skins available. And with news around Galaxy OS, I expect it to keep the flow in the same direction. But these small changes and settings are what users look for in a UI to differentiate it from thousands of other similar phones. From my experience, I have learned one thing: software updates can improve a phone while quietly changing the preferences I made. From now on, I will check my preferences after each major update rather than wait for the change to show up.

item.title: I put a temperature sensor in every room, and my thermostat had been lying about my house for years
item.itunes:title: I put a temperature sensor in every room, and my thermostat had been lying about my house for years
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My smart thermostat was one of the first devices I added to my smart home, a 3rd-gen Nest Learning Thermostat at launch. It moved with me from that apartment to a house, and I thought it was doing a great job. So I've fixed other things in my smart home, like getting power delivery sorted and adding controls to Home Assistant for centralized ease of use.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But the thermostat was silently sabotaging things. Never mind that it couldn't tell if my windows were open; it was also deciding the whole house's temperature from one place. As it turns out, the wrong place. Sure, the living room wall that it's on is part of an open-plan setup that is the entire floor. But I'm in a three-floor townhome, and that makes the basement and upper floor never comfortable.

I pay for exactly one smart home subscription, and it's the one built so I can cancel it without losing anything

I don't want to be locked into paying monthly for essential features

By  Jasmine Mannan

One wall was deciding the temperature for the whole house

Your thermostat is usually in the wrong place

Thermostat placement hasn't changed much since their invention. Place it on a central wall, where people can reach it easily, and hope for the best. Mine is on the living room wall, on a floor with no dividing walls, underneath one of the central air return vents. That's textbook "right" placement, with airflow and no direct sunlight to mess up the readings.

But in an open-plan space like that with two staircases, it's also an easy place for the thermostat to be wrong. It's simple physics. Cool air sinks, warm air rises.

The only usual temperature bias that applies here is the return grille above it. It's not in direct sun even with the curtains open, it's not on an external wall (and it's a new build so well-insulated anyway), and it's not a small hallway. In the apartment, it was also in an open-plan area, but with a much smaller area to handle.

So I carried a sensor through the house to check

I picked up a Nest Sensor, paired it to the thermostat, and moved it around the house to see how big the temperature swing was between the centrally placed thermostat and those areas. I kept the sensor in the area for 20 minutes or so, so it could acclimatize, and kept the thermostat as the controller for the AC.

Room

Sensor reading

Living room (open-plan main floor)

70°F

Downstairs hallway

71°F

Main bedroom

72°F

Office

73°F

Upstairs hallway

74°F

Also, I did this at night after the sun had gone down. I'm sure the temperature swings would have been higher during the day, especially in the upstairs hallway and main bedroom, both of which have terrible air circulation.

That's a 4-degree swing between the living room and the warmest part of the house, and it could have been higher. I have a temperature sensor and air sensor on my office desk, and it's regularly 78F or higher when the thermostat is set to 74F.

7 sensors under $10 that completely changed my smart home

You don't need to splurge to build a smart home

29
By  Samir Makwana

Telling the Nest to listen to a different room only half fixes it

What the sensor actually does on a 3rd gen (and what it doesn't)

The Nest Sensor is the best thing I added to the thermostat, but it can only do so much. It uses BLE, so it drops connectivity from the thermostat in some areas of the house, and I've had to move it around to find the optimal signal. Having a second room as the control temperature for the AC or heating means the rooms we're in during the day can be more comfortable. The only snag is that I work in the basement office, and my wife works on the top floor. That means only one of us can be at the temperature we like.

Buying more sensors won't help either. My 3rd-gen can support up to six, but only one is active at any time. The sensors also don't have occupancy sensors, so they run purely on temperature.

But even with one sensor, where you place it really matters. If I put it in the upstairs hallway, the AC would run forever, trying to cool down an area with low air circulation and no register. Putting it in the bedrooms keeps you comfortable at night, but not much during the day.

3 stunning ESP32 E Ink display projects you can make this weekend

Why settle for a regular screen when an e-ink one can do it better?

3
By  Simon Batt

A thermostat that only trusts one room at a time is still guessing

One sensor was enough to show the problem but not enough to fix it

A single paired sensor is good for diagnosing temperature differences between rooms, but it's not that useful for daily life. And my thermostat is aging out of support, so there's no point buying more sensors when I'm not sure if I'll stay in the Google ecosystem. The 4th-gen does average across rooms, but if I'm upgrading, it'll be HomeKit-compatible, since more of my devices play nice with that.

I can make things somewhat more comfortable by using a sensor schedule, but even then it's blindly following a schedule and not paying attention to how we're using the space. Whichever floor the sensor isn't on will drift by several degrees, which is fine in spring and fall but not when it's either cold or hot outside.

And the other thing is that I'm doing my best to get everything running in Home Assistant. That means picking a thermostat that works well with it, and that's probably going to be something that isn't from Google or Amazon.

Your smart home temperature sensors are useless if you don't calibrate them

What use is a sensor that's wrong?

2
By  Jasmine Mannan

My thermostat still lies to my AC, but I know better

I always wondered why I wasn't comfortable in the office, but now I know. And even with an attached sensor, it's hard to keep every floor at a comfortable temperature from a single central air handler. Maybe I'll add a portable AC unit for the office to help keep the computers cool, but otherwise the sensor stays down here to drive the AC where it's needed.

item.itunes:title: I tried OpenClaw and Perplexity Computer, but ChatGPT Dots finally feels like a personal assistant
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We've reached a pretty dystopian point where people will casually say they asked "Chat" a question, and everyone around them knows exactly who they're talking about. Not a friend, not a colleague, but an AI chatbot. Somehow, we've gone from Googling everything to treating ChatGPT like that one friend who knows a little bit about everything.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That said, we've now gone one step beyond just asking "Chat" questions and getting answers. We've officially stepped into an even more dystopian era where AI isn't just waiting for us to ask questions anymore. It's keeping tabs on our lives, remembering things we'd forgotten ourselves, and reaching out to us before we even realize we need help. In other words, we've gone from talking to AI to having AI initiate conversations with us.

I've been actively trying out tools built around this premise, including OpenClaw and Perplexity Computer. I've been putting ChatGPT's recently launched Dots through its paces for the last three weeks, and it might just beat them all.

Dots makes having a personal AI assistant feel effortless

You don't need to be a tech nerd to use Dots

Always-on AI agents that actually take initiative to do the work for you have been around for months now. Despite that, they've clearly not been as widely adopted as conventional AI chatbots, and I think a big part of that comes down to how complicated they can be to set up and use.

Take OpenClaw, for example. While getting started has become considerably easier with dedicated installers for macOS and Windows, it previously required running loads of commands in the terminal. Despite the installers, though, there's still a learning curve involved when it comes to configuring the agent and connecting it with the tools you rely on daily. For someone who just wants an AI assistant that works out of the box, that can be a lot to ask.

This is where Dots comes in. Announced at OpenAI's annual DevDay conference, Dots are what the company describes as "remarkably capable, always-on agents built to handle everything." Powered by GPT-6 Astra, each Dot has its own cloud computer and browser, can connect to thousands of apps, and is designed to work on your behalf around the clock.

Before I talk about Dots' capabilities and how I've been using it as my personal assistant, I think the most important thing to highlight is just how effortless it is to get started with. Unlike OpenClaw, Dots doesn't require you to spend hours setting things up or figuring out an entirely new interface. The setup involves very basic tasks, like choosing a name for your Dot and customizing how it looks. It's available on ChatGPT's web interface, desktop app, and mobile apps right out of the box, too.

Ultimately, you don't need any technical knowledge to get started, beyond knowing how to navigate the same old ChatGPT interface you've probably been using for years.

The proactiveness is where Dots really shines

Dots knows when to step in without being asked

When Dots was launched, I saw a lot of people sharing that they'd been using AI chatbots as their personal assistants long before Dots came along. While that's certainly true, I think there's a pretty big difference between the two. For the most part, using a conventional AI chatbot as a personal assistant involves an active back-and-forth. You feed it a prompt, it gives you an answer, and you repeat the process whenever you need something else done.

Now, you could technically make a chatbot proactive by setting up scheduled tasks, reminders, or automations that monitor certain things for you. ChatGPT itself has supported these features for quite some time now. But even then, there's a limitation to that proactiveness. You're still the one who has to figure out what needs monitoring in the first place and tell the chatbot what to look out for.

That's where Dots has really changed things for me. Rather than waiting for you to identify a potential problem or tell it what needs doing, it can proactively look through information from your connected apps, figure out what might need your attention, and reach out to you about it. After using it for three weeks, I'd argue that this is easily its most impressive aspect.

I stopped typing to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for a week, and discovered a better way to use AI

I gave my fingers a break and my AI chats got better

4
By  Mahnoor Faisal

For instance, I have a group project for a course I'm taking where we need to reach out to multiple organizations to set up a seminar. I remember starting a ChatGPT thread and asking it to help me find organizations we could reach out to, and I didn't think much of it afterward. It was just another conversation I'd had with ChatGPT, and as far as I was concerned, it was over.

A few days later, though, I got a notification from my Dot telling me that one of the organizations we'd reached out to had replied. Not only did it summarize their response, including how many people they wanted the session for and when they were hoping to schedule it, but it also offered to help me plan the workshop activities.

To be clear, I hadn't asked my Dot to keep tabs on this project, nor had I set up any automations or reminders to monitor my inbox for replies. It had simply picked up on something I was working on and recognized that an email I'd received was relevant to it. That's exactly the kind of proactiveness I think sets Dots apart.

Dots learns more about you as you use it

The more you use Dots, the better it understands you

In addition to taking initiative and proactively reaching out to you, another reason why using Dots has really grown on me is because of how useful it gets over time. Similar to memory in ChatGPT, Dots begins to pick up on your habits and preferences, gradually learning how you work, what matters to you, and the things you tend to need help with. The more you interact with it, the better it gets at understanding your routines and anticipating what you might need without you having to explain everything from scratch each time.

For instance, an example I mentioned in another article about Dots' proactiveness was how I made a bit of a financial blunder and accidentally withdrew a significantly larger amount from my Payoneer account than intended. Naturally, I was pretty stressed about the whole situation, and Dots helped me keep track of my correspondence with Payoneer's support team.

What's interesting, though, is that Dots seems to have picked up on the fact that withdrawals from this account are something I tend to worry about. Ever since that incident, it's started notifying me whenever I make a withdrawal from Payoneer, something it never did before the scare. I hadn't asked it to monitor my withdrawals going forward, either. It had seemingly picked up on something that caused me a lot of stress and started keeping an eye on it.

Similarly, I've been using Dots quite a bit for studying lately. Over time, it's started picking up on how I prefer to study, the courses I'm taking, and the kind of help I typically need when preparing for exams.

So, instead of having to explain my study routine or provide context about my courses every time, it already has a pretty good idea of what I'm working on and how I like to approach it.

There's a catch (and a pretty big silver lining)

The biggest downside here is that Dots is currently exclusive to ChatGPT Pro subscriptions and above. This means you're looking at a subscription costing at least $100 a month just to get access to it. Of course, if you already pay for the Pro tier, this is just another benefit you're getting at no additional cost. However, for someone who doesn't, that's a pretty steep price to pay for a personal AI assistant regardless of how impressive it might be.

The silver lining, though, is that the usage limits have been surprisingly generous so far. Conversations with your Dot don't count toward your regular ChatGPT usage limits, although tasks it delegates to ChatGPT Work or Codex do. OpenAI has also been offering extended usage allowances during the initial rollout, which might explain why I've been able to use it so extensively without running into major limitations.

These introductory allowances aren't necessarily representative of what using Dots will look like in the long run, and OpenAI hasn't clearly outlined exactly how much autonomous work users will be able to get out of their subscriptions once the promotional period ends.

item.itunes:title: Claude blamed my RTX 5080’s VRAM for crashes, but the real culprit was far more surprising
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For about three months, my PC had a nasty crashing habit that I could not nail down. Games would crash, but not consistently, and not in a way I could reproduce. I had a couple of blue-screens at idle and under load, and since I never experienced a total crash on Linux, I attributed them to Windows bugginess. And as far as the frequency goes, it wasn't enough to be bothersome, until a couple of weeks ago.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I couldn't make it 10 minutes into a gaming session without a complete crash, and I knew it was time I had to get to the bottom of it. I gave all of my evidence to Claude—game crash logs, Windows logs, and anything else I could find, and it confidently diagnosed my pre-owned RTX 5080's VRAM as the issue. I was halfway to an RMA before I took a closer look at what it found, and the true cause ended up being my system memory configuration, which hadn't changed since I built my system years ago.

My crazy powerful gaming PC feels like a ticking time bomb

We shouldn't have to worry that high-end hardware will burn itself up.

8
By  Jacob Roach

Claude was great at the tedious part

I'll never hunt through logs myself ever again

I'll give Claude credit where it's due, because its ability to triage the problem was incredibly helpful. I was experiencing crashing in Escape From Tarkov, and that game writes detailed crash logs for nearly every subsystem for a single session. I handed Claude the entire folder, and it parsed through all of it and found the thing that mattered in under a minute.

It found a "DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED" error, which is Windows telling you the GPU stopped responding and the driver had to reset it. At best, this causes game crash; at worst, this could cause a system crash. From there it walked me through PowerShell commands that could dig into Windows' event history. This dug up an NVIDIA driver reset logged one second before Tarkov’s first error, a kernel watchdog dump written at the same moment, a set of graphics exceptions complaining about a corrupt “shader program header,” and three more resets going back to August.

Those dates all lined up exactly with crashes I had experienced, and at least at this point, all signs pointed to the GPU being the culprit.

24GB VRAM should be the new minimum for most GPUs
64
By  Rich Edmonds

One flipped bit became the whole diagnosis

A red herring

The next step was a GPU memory test. Claude pointed me at memtest_vulkan, a free tool that fills video memory with patterns and checks that they read back correctly. About 45 seconds into the first run, it caught a single flipped bit, and this became the catalyst for the whole set of events that followed.

Claude then told me that the flipped bit was evidence of a VRAM defect and that I should start an RMA process with MSI. When I asked why a card that had been fine for months would suddenly start failing, it claimed that the error sat about 13GB into the card’s 16GB of memory, so maybe a recent game update had pushed Tarkov high enough to start landing on a weak spot. That didn't really make sense to me, since other games that fill the buffer completely weren't reliably crashing, so I took a closer look at the test results myself, and that opened up a whole new can of worms.

4 myths about VRAM you shouldn’t believe

The VRAM conversation is more nuanced than you think.

13
By  Ty Sherback

The number that Claude missed that pointed to the true cause

The speed was a huge red flag

The VRAM test I had been using reports throughput as it runs, and my failing runs were moving data at somewhere between 200 and 300GB/s. The RTX 5080’s memory is rated for 960GB/s, so that already raised some suspicion. A test that’s actually hammering the card’s VRAM should land somewhere near that, and eventually one did: a clean run hit roughly 850GB/s and passed for about three hours, with the memory overclocked above stock.

This clear run, to me, was a big red flag with the RMA suggestion. Claude did catch this huge delta between tests, but it attributed it to clock states, and it also didn't properly parse through the test screenshot alongside HWiNFO, which showed that the PCIe bus was under significant load with the failing tests at lower speeds. This should've been a clear-cut sign that either the PCIe bus or system's RAM was extremely suspect.

When video memory runs out, Windows quietly pages data out to system RAM rather than refusing the request. When I had started the initial test there were apps that were holding a few gigabytes of my VRAM, so part of memtest’s buffer ended up in system memory, and that's likely where the problem was. I ran an overnight VRAM test, and when that turned up no errors, I knew exactly where to look next.

I had Claude look into my Windows 11 PC, and it revealed problems I didn’t know I had

"Hey Claude, what's wrong with my PC?"

3
By  Abhinav Raj

My RAM was the prime suspect

More DDR5 instability

My PC runs a Ryzen 7 7800X3D with four 16GB sticks of DDR5-6000, which doesn't sound crazy, but AMD only rates Ryzen 7000 CPUs for up to 5200 on two sticks, and drops that speed to 3600MT/s once all four slots are filled. Cranking the speed up to 6000 didn't seem ridiculous since that's what AMD itself called the "sweet spot" for Zen 4 chips, but going from 5200MT/s to 6000MT/s on two sticks is an entirely different ask compared to going from 3600MT/s to 6000MT/s.

This was the memory configuration I had run since I put together this PC in 2024, but the evidence was pointing to this being the cause, so I ran an overnight memory test.

And there it was: MemTest86+ reported 22 errors after five hours of clean passes, and that was the smoking gun behind everything.

I haven't had the time to test every combination of sticks to see if one may be faulty, but the most likely explanation is that four DIMMs at that speed were just asking far too much of my CPU's memory controller. Instead of dropping the speed and sacrificing performance, I took out two sticks, and Tarkov has been stable ever since.

Hardware prices have me avoiding any sort of overclocking

By  Samarveer Singh

Using AI to troubleshoot isn't a bad idea, but it can still miss the small details

For first-line troubleshooting, I'm still reaching for an AI model because it's the fastest way to parse through a pile of logs to find the relevant errors. But for the testing portion, I'm trusting my own knowledge and gut instinct. When it comes to errors like this, the cause can be complex and multi-faceted, and you're never really sure based on just one piece of evidence. Before acting on an AI's diagnosis with something drastic like an RMA, running a test to rule out other components is always a good idea, and I almost learned that the hard way.

item.title: The beginner-friendly Bambu Lab P1S 3D printer is at its lowest price ever
item.itunes:title: The beginner-friendly Bambu Lab P1S 3D printer is at its lowest price ever
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
3D printing has moved far beyond the tinkering-heavy days of DIY kits, and the Bambu Lab P1S is a big reason why. This enclosed, CoreXY printer brings high-speed printing and automatic calibration to a price point that actually makes sense for beginners and hobbyists alike. With the ability to get you from idea to finished piece in just 15 minutes, it's a perfect introduction to 3D printing.

Get started with 3D printing with this Bambu Labs printer.

See at Amazon

Right now, you can grab the base model of the Bambu Lab P1S for just $349 on Amazon, down from its regular $399 price. This $50 discount is the lowest price we’ve seen, making it an ideal time to step into reliable, high-speed FDM printing. While it lacks the multicolor AMS system included in the combo version, the base unit offers all the core performance features that have made Bambu Lab’s ecosystem so popular.

Why the Bambu Lab P1S is a smart buy for beginners

An easy-to-use, budget 3D printer

The P1S stands out because it removes the friction usually associated with getting started. The fully enclosed chamber isn't just for looks; it allows the printer to handle advanced filaments like ABS and ASA, which warp easily on open-frame machines. You also get automatic bed leveling and vibration compensation, meaning you don’t have to manually adjust the bed or tune input shaping settings to get clean first layers.

Performance-wise, the P1S is no slouch. It features a CoreXY motion system capable of 500mm/s print speeds and 20,000 mm/s² acceleration. This means large prints that might take hours on a budget printer are often done in a fraction of the time. The 256 x 256 x 256 mm build volume is generous for its class, fitting most hobbyist projects without taking up too much desk space.

If you’re looking to add multicolor capabilities later, the P1S is fully compatible with Bambu Lab’s AMS (Automatic Material System) units, allowing you to print in up to 16 colors. But since this is just the base model, it’s best viewed as a high-performance single-color workhorse. It offers the speed and reliability of Bambu’s premium X1 series but at a much more accessible entry point.

This is the lowest we’ve seen the base model drop to, so if you’ve been waiting to jump into 3D printing, now is the moment to act.
